title: Homily on the Leave-taking of the Dormition

pairs.en: On this present day the Holy Church celebrates the leave-taking of the feast of the Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos. Small and unworthy as we are in comparison with her, yet our own falling asleep, too, will in all likelihood be followed by a leave-taking of its own kind; that is, after our death as well, according to the Rule of the Holy Church, our memory will be kept in prayer on the third, the ninth, and the fortieth day, with “memory eternal” proclaimed for us each time.
When will this be, and will it be soon? No one knows. Perhaps very soon indeed. But in any case even the most distant death stands only a few decades away — no more.

sections.heading: Soon we shall not be here

pairs.en: And so a little time will pass, and we shall no longer be on earth! A little time will pass, and this present world, with all its goods and all its griefs, will cease to exist for us!

Where, then, shall we be? We shall be where all our forefathers now are, and where all our descendants will pass after us. We shall be where none of us enters alive, and from which none returns dead. We shall be where for some there is neither sorrow nor sighing, and for others neither joy nor rest. We shall be where it is not as in this world, where everything that begins comes to an end, but where whatever has once begun exists without end. That is where we shall all be in a few years!..

Do we think of this, brethren? Are we preparing ourselves for the new dwelling in heaven, for a mode of existence higher and unending? So little, that this subject does not belong at all to the ordinary circle of our reflection. Incomprehensible strangeness! Astonishing carelessness! If some journey to a distant land lies ahead — what gatherings and preparations there are! We try to learn in advance about the place to which we are going: who lives there, what the customs are, what the country is like, what the conveniences and inconveniences of life there may be; we try to have in store everything that could be of use to us; we establish connections and acquaintances there beforehand.
But to enter eternity! To furnish ourselves with what will be necessary for us there! To free ourselves in good time from what is not tolerated there! Of this we have neither thought nor care...

What does this mean? Can it be unbelief in the life to come? But how can one fail to believe it, when our very life here is plainly only a beginning, which necessarily presupposes a continuation? How can one fail to believe in life beyond the grave, when in the best moments of our life we ourselves not only feel that there is within us something not of this world, but, one may say, already have a foretaste of the life that awaits us in eternity?

Or perhaps someone thinks that it makes no difference how one enters eternity — having prepared for it, or without preparing at all? But to reason in this way is to have less sense than a child. For it is evident that the life to come must stand in close and immediate connection with the present one, as the fruit with the flower, as the flower with the stem. What is sown here will be reaped there. *He that soweth to his flesh* — let us say it in the words of the holy Paul — *shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting* (Gal. 6:8). To hope for the contrary would be to overturn in one's own thoughts the ordinance of God's wisdom and righteousness, the order of all nature.

What, then — let us ask once more — what does our carelessness mean with regard to the eternity that awaits us? It means that we, like little children who have lost themselves gazing at their toys, forget everything, even our very selves; it means that the world has so dazzled us and bound us to itself that we dare not even think of anything else besides the satisfaction of our senses, our whims, and our passions. For one of our greatest misfortunes is this: that we have the capacity, while busying ourselves with a trifle, to leave the most important thing at that very moment without attention. It is because of this that we so unreasonably prize earthly gains or losses, and are so inattentive to what awaits us in eternity!

Are we to remain forever in this strange and ruinous neglect of eternity? Immortal soul, soul destined to dwell with God Himself! How long will you lie as one dead and without feeling? Arise — why do you sleep? You sleep and give yourself up to the dreams of your imagination, while death is already preparing to snatch you from among the living. Rouse yourself, then, while there is yet time; rouse yourself, survey your perilous position, and, like a traveller who has fallen asleep on the road, take up the staff of faith and press on along the path of virtue to that place where there is neither sorrow nor sighing! Amen.

sections.heading: Turning to the Protection of the Mother of God

pairs.en: That the present festival is one of the most joyful, for it shows the intercession of the Mother of God for us before God; that for this very reason the present day ought to be spent in works of piety and Christian love, so that we may be counted worthy of the protection of the Most Blessed one; that all who neglect their salvation cannot, until they amend themselves, have any just hope in her intercession before God — these important and needful truths are, without doubt, more or less known to each of us. Let us therefore turn our attention to something else: let us look at the very manner of the Mother of God's protecting veil, and see whether some new lesson for us may not be found in it.

Do you remember, brethren, how the wondrous event we now commemorate came to pass?.. In the Blachernae church of Constantinople, on the eve of the Lord's day, the usual all-night vigil was being celebrated, and among those present was Saint Andrew, the fool for Christ's sake. In the midst of the hymns and prayers this man of God, at the fourth hour of the night, suddenly beheld in the air the Mother of God, with the Forerunner of Christ and John the Theologian, amid a multitude of angels and saints, praying for the human race and covering the people in the church with her most pure omophorion. Filled with spiritual joy, the seer turned to his friend and disciple in the spirit, Saint Epiphanius, and asked him whether he saw the wonder. “I see it, father,” answered Epiphanius, “and I am struck with awe.” When the rest of those present in the church learned of this miracle, a joyful trembling seized them all; with contrite hearts they began to thank God and to glorify the Protectress of the whole world, and the pious emperor Leo and the holy patriarch Tarasius ordained that this consoling event be commemorated every year.

sections.heading: The heavenly hosts care for us

pairs.en: The first thing on which we ought to fix our attention here is the very appearance of the Mother of God with the choirs of angels and saints.

So it is not in vain that we believe that the dwellers of heaven take a great part in the events of the human world, that our elder brethren in heaven care for the salvation of us, their little ones, on earth! To what better use could they put their power and their nearness to the throne of grace, if not to help us, tossed as we are on the sea of life's misfortunes and cares? Even we, for all the coldness of the earthly heart, cannot look without sympathy upon the unfortunate, and not seldom we render them help; shall heavenly beings, then, remain idle spectators of our spiritual and bodily poverty, and not spread over us their grace-filled protection!

It is not in vain, therefore, that we also believe that the heavenly powers are present with us in the churches! Where should they dwell more constantly than where their King and Lord is especially present? We do not see them, because the radiance of heavenly glory is unbearable to the eye of clay; but they see us and all that is ours — our very thoughts and desires. The time will come, and we shall see them; we shall enter, if we prove worthy of it, into their own most radiant circle; but until that time we must believe in their invisible presence and, believing, visit the churches of God as often as we can. Only, brethren, if we desire to be in the churches with the angels, we must also stand in the churches in the manner of angels, having laid aside “all earthly care”. Otherwise the tempter can appear even in paradise, and even in paradise one can earn that terrible sentence: *ye shall surely die!* (Gen. 2:17).

The second thing deserving of devout attention in the appearance of the Mother of God is the form in which she showed herself in the air to the seers. As the Mother of the King of Heaven, she could have appeared seated upon a throne, sending down blessings from its height upon the human race; but she appears — praying! Why so? That we may understand that there is one supreme Master of all things, in heaven and on earth, in time and in eternity — God the Father! One Redeemer, Proclaimer of the will of God, Lawgiver and Judge, *who is able to save and to destroy* (James 4:12) — God the Son! One Comforter and Giver of the gifts of grace, Sanctifier of repentant sinners — God the Holy Spirit! What, then, is the Most Holy Virgin? The foremost heir of grace and the first intercessor at His throne for the human race. Whoever sends up his prayers to her in this spirit will act in accordance with her own desire. On the contrary, a veneration of her name carried to excess — to the point of comparing it with the name of God, to the detriment of that reverence which we owe our Creator and Redeemer — would constitute not an honour but an offence to her who, having named herself on earth “the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1:38), has without doubt not abandoned that humility in heaven. *See thou do it not,* said the angel once to the apostle John, who had, it seems, taken him for the God-man and wished to honour him with divine honour — *for I am thy fellowservant... worship God* (Rev. 22:9). The same, and with still greater force, would the Most Holy Virgin say to anyone who, through lack of understanding, should begin to render her worship equal to that which is due to God.

But is there much need today to fear an excess of devotion to the Most Holy Virgin? Alas, in our time one must rather fear its lack! The Mother will herself render to the Son, on our behalf, what belongs to Him. Let us rather learn from her the thing of which we have the greatest need — prayer.

If even in heaven nothing can be done without prayer, if prayer is needed even for her who is more honourable than the Cherubim and beyond compare more glorious than the Seraphim, then how necessary, brethren, is prayer for us! And how much, therefore, do they lose who neglect this gift of God! And many do neglect it! There are people who do not pray at all. Others pray, but under compulsion, with a sense of burden. Prayer seems to them a heavy tribute — labour rendered to a master. And indeed, to pray without feeling the need of prayer, without knowing why or for what one prays, is heavy work. But who is to blame that the manna of heaven turns to bitterness in our mouths? True prayer is sweet and nourishing, and there is no one among those who pray who has not at some time tasted this sweetness. If prayer becomes bitter, it is because our spiritual taste has been spoiled. It is hard for us to lift our eyes to heaven because they are covered over with the dust of earthly cares. A man dying of hunger will cry out and demand food the moment he sees another human being; a drowning man stretches out his hands even to lifeless things; in the same way, whoever comes to feel spiritual hunger will find his lips opening of themselves in prayer; whoever sees himself in the abyss of sin will find his eyes and hands rising to heaven of their own accord.

“How is one to awaken in oneself the feeling of this hunger — of this danger? How is one to make oneself see one's need of God?” By turning strict attention upon oneself and one's own life. Try to reflect for a few hours — I do not even say days — on how we come into the world, why we appear in it, and what awaits us in that place to which we shall go afterwards. It cannot be that such reflection should fail to end with eyes turned toward heaven, with a heartfelt sigh before the All-Knowing One, in whose right hand are our being and our life. The more often you repeat this good exercise and think upon your destiny for eternity, examine your life and see your sins and impurity, the more you will feel the need of heavenly help and mercy; prayer will become ever more necessary and more pleasant to you; and in time you will attain also that holy disposition — to be always in the presence of God — which the apostle calls “praying without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17).

sections.heading: Who was found worthy to see the vision

pairs.en: Let us now look at those people who were counted worthy to behold the Protection of the Most Holy Virgin. In the church of Blachernae there was a multitude of people; there was an emperor, surnamed the Wise for his learning; there was a patriarch who was afterwards, for the holiness of his life, numbered among the saints; there were people of renown and wealth — yet none of them saw what was taking place in the air. Only Andrew and Epiphanius were counted worthy to be witnesses of the miracle — men of the very lowest station, despised by many during their earthly life. So near and so open is heaven to everyone who is worthy, though among men he be nothing!

From the circumstances of the appearance it is not even evident that it was pointed out to the holy seers in some manner from above, or that their spiritual eye was opened for the occasion by some special power of God. Their ascetic life and unceasing self-denial had so refined their spiritual senses that the presence of heavenly beings could not remain hidden from them. So it commonly is with great ascetics: rare is the one among them who does not possess the gift of spiritual sight — a gift that belongs to all men, but which in the unregenerate is crushed beneath the weight of the flesh.

sections.heading: The fool who saw what is above all reason

pairs.en: A particularly remarkable trait in the character of Saint Andrew is that he was a fool; that is, for Christ's sake he appeared to be deprived of reason. And behold, it is this man, deprived of reason, who is the first to see what is above all reason! Let us not draw from this anything to the disparagement of the human mind, as a faculty given by God and forming the adornment of our soul; nor let us draw from it unfavourable conclusions about human learning, which likewise comes from God and which, sanctified by grace, not only serves our earthly wellbeing but assists us also on the way to heaven. Yet how can we fail to note here what has been noted so many times and is impressed with such force in the word of God: that human wisdom, for its almost perpetual errors, is accounted by God “foolishness” (1 Cor. 1:20), and is therefore condemned to be “destroyed” (1 Cor. 1:19)!.. There is something in earthly wisdom that makes it little capable of receiving illuminations from above; there is in the fallen human mind some dark side, hostile to heaven. What is it?.. What makes earthly wisdom, which in itself ought to be praiseworthy, hateful to God? Why does human reason, in itself godlike, become unlike God? Where is the beginning of the evil? In what the apostle calls the mind's being “puffed up” (1 Cor. 8:1) — its conceit. Filled with the light of knowledge, the mind naturally begins to shine; but this shining, because of the diseased state of the mind's eyes in fallen man, for the most part blinds him; and instead of beholding with gratitude and humility the light within God's light, he begins to think that the radiance he gives off is his own. From this comes the dangerous feeling of self-satisfaction and the forgetting of one's own poverty; then the pretension to omniscience and resistance to the divine revelations and mysteries; then the forgetting of God, contempt for the Church, and disrespect for the public order; then the weakening of conscience and slavery to sensuality; and then doubt about sacred things — even about what constitutes the proper dignity of human nature itself; and men who began by claiming that they know everything, that they stand above everything, often end by doubting their own existence, placing themselves on a level with the dumb beasts! Thus earthly wisdom makes a fool of itself and destroys itself even before it is destroyed by the God of knowledge (1 Sam. 2:3).

Is it any wonder, after this, that such wisdom is condemned to destruction? Such a passage from knowledge to impiety is in itself unnatural, for earthly light ought to lead to the Heavenly Light, and the human mind ought to turn man toward the mind of God; but since, through the corruption of men, the contrary almost always happens, then — so as not to be delayed, one might say, by a fruitless sorting of what in human wisdom deserves to be spared and what does not — it has been made a rule with God that everyone who desires salvation should renounce earthly wisdom and become foolish for Christ's sake. *If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise* (1 Cor. 3:18). Consent or refusal to cast off one's own wisdom, being a condition of salvation, is at the same time an unfailing sign of whether a man's wisdom was true or false. He who possessed true wisdom will at once exchange it for the wisdom of grace, and is always ready to take his mind captive into the obedience of the mind of God; but he whose wisdom was sick with conceit finds it very hard to leave it behind. And this leaving is either open or hidden. The open form we see in the fools for Christ's sake: in them there is a complete renunciation of the mind — a lofty ascetic feat, accessible to few, not only because to appear voluntarily deprived of reason is exceedingly hard for our self-loving heart, but also because in such a feat a man wavers unceasingly between two dangers: that of betraying his holy vow of foolishness for Christ's sake, and that of violating the duty of love toward his neighbour — by giving him scandal, or by withholding needed counsel from him, or in some other way. But one can be a fool for Christ's sake without appearing deprived of reason, even while making use of all the riches of human wisdom. The apostle Paul was a *fool for Christ's sake* (1 Cor. 4:10), yet he taught the philosophers in the Areopagus! The hierarchs Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom were luminaries of their age, and yet they were not strangers to the foolishness of Christ. All this comes about through humility for Christ's sake: humility reconciles earthly wisdom with the foolishness of Christ. He who is guided by humility looks upon all his knowledge, first of all, as an unmerited gift of God, and therefore he has no ground for conceit. And besides, earthly wisdom itself, proceeding rightly in such a man, soon brings him to the limits of human knowledge; and, unable to step beyond them, yet feeling the need to go further, it hands its pupil over to faith — that is, it yields its place to the holy “foolishness of God” (1 Cor. 1:25).

sections.heading: True wisdom made foolish for Christ

pairs.en: Before such men — wise in the eyes of the world and at the same time fools in the eyes of God — the mysteries of the spiritual world were laid open, as their lives bear witness, with the same readiness as before those who for Christ's sake appeared to the world utterly deprived of reason.

sections.heading: A homily to be finished by your own reflection

pairs.en: One might touch on still other circumstances of the miraculous appearance of the Most Holy Virgin which we commemorate today: for instance, why was the vision not noticed even by such a man as the patriarch Tarasius? Why was Saint Andrew, as he contemplated the vision, filled more with joy, while Saint Epiphanius was filled more with fear? But something must be left to the personal reflection of each one of you. The aim of Christian instruction ought to consist not in communicating everything possible concerning the subject under consideration, but also in awakening the hearers' own reflection. For him who joins his own reflection to what he hears, much comes even out of little; while for him who only listens and does not reflect at all himself, even much proves useless.
And so, in place of a conclusion to this homily, accept from me a request: prolong it by your own reflection.
And upon this good work may the blessing of the Lord be with you all! Amen.
